utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Good morning, everybody. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present today. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Ms. Condon. Mr. Zivanovic, she was supposed to be here today or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Condon is coming today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic should be here today, or he'll be working in the office and be here tomorrow for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And for the Prosecution, I just notice Mr. Vanderpuye. So good morning. I understand, Mr. Bourgon, you'd like to address the Chamber on some preliminary issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before I do so, Mr. President, I'd just like to introduce a newcomer on our team. Mr. Anthony Battah will be doing his articling with our team starting as of 15 June until 15 September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Judges. Good morning, colleagues. At this point in time, Mr. President, I would like to make an oral motion regarding Witness 128 which is due to testify in the coming days. Witness 128, Mr. President -- I don't think there is a need to go into private session. I will simply use the number 128 and nothing else. This witness, Mr. President, was met by the Prosecution on three different occasions for interviews. On the first two occasions, while the witness was not a suspect, the interviews were recorded and we have been provided with transcripts of the interviews. The third time he was met, and that was in October of 2002 - I'm into the sure about the date; I do not have the papers with me this morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But this -- on the third time he was, that was in Banja Luka, and he was interviewed for a period of four hours by the Office of the Prosecution in the presence of Mr. McCloskey, my colleague from the Prosecution. The exact date, Mr. President, is 29 October 2002. The result of that interview, the Defence has been provided only with an info report which contains three pages, basically a summary of the four hours during which the witness was interviewed. From the info report, we learn that the witness was a suspect from 15.27, or 3 hours 27, until 18.03, three minutes after 6.00. Basically, for a period of some two and a half hours, he was made a suspect, and then the suspect status was then withdrawn. So from witness he became suspect and back to a witness once the Prosecution was satisfied with his answers. Pursuant to Rule 43, of course, whenever a witness becomes a suspect, there is an obligation that the interview be recorded, and in this case, we have asked the Prosecution to provide us with the interview. We have been in contact over the weekend with the Prosecution. We do not have a final answer yet, so it may be that this oral motion is not really necessary. If there was, indeed, an interview and they can give it to us, then it's foreclosed. However, should the interview not be -- should the interview not have been recorded, we believe, Mr. President, that this is a clear violation of Rule 43, and the remedy that we ask for in these circumstances, in order to allow us to do our work properly and to prepare for this witness, is to obtain all the notes that were taken during this interview, at least during the period when the witness was a suspect. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you very much. The Beara Defence team joins in on that motion wholeheartedly, and even if the notes are available, we still believe that we would like to have the tape-recording or transcript of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like also to join this motion. I asked for this transcript from the Prosecution already but I haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a matter of principle and we also join in the submission of Mr. Bourgon. But the Defence team of Mr. Miletic has already asked for clarification and a transcript from the OTP in case this recording is not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On principle, we would also like to join Mr. Bourgon's motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau, and thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau, you said have asked already, put in a request to the Prosecution. When was that, and did you have a reply?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, it was only last Saturday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you haven't had a reply, I suppose. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may add, our request also dates this weekend. That's why I'm not surprised of not having received an answer at this time yet, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfectly understandable, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good morning to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to my colleagues as well. Mr. President, I don't know that much about this situation. I did have an opportunity to speak to Mr. Nicholls yesterday and my understanding is that he's still looking into the question of whether or not a tape-recording exists of this interview. So it may very well be that the issue would be mooted out to the extent that one might exist. But I would prefer, with your indulgence, to allow Mr. Nicholls the opportunity to address this matter. I think he's in a far better position than I am to address this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. I called on you to respond because you happen to be the only one present this morning. So perhaps you could communicate to Mr. Nicholls, actually, the need for his presence at some point in time during today's sitting so that we can clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in case the tape-recording does not exist, then what's your response to the request that has been made by the various Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, I'd prefer Mr. Nicholls to address it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want Mr. Nicholls to address that, not you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll let him know that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can bring the witness -- yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There is a second issue concerning Witness 128 which I'd like to raise. I will not raise it at this time but it regards the Rule 65 ter summary which was produced for this witness. And I need to speak to my colleague before I do, but it is important for me to put this on the record, that there is something I will be talking to the Prosecution about concerning the information which was used in order to produce the Rule 65 ter summary. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So let's bring the witness in, please. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I didn't want to interrupt my colleague, but I really have no access to the LiveNote. It's not working on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with that straight away. Is there anyone else who has got problems with LiveNote?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently it's okay now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thanks, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have a problem with LiveNote, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've been infected by Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll deal with it, Mr. Zivanovic. In the meantime, can I swear in the -- can I proceed with the swearing in of the witness? Good morning to you, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a restful weekend and that you are fresh, to the extent that you can face another barrage of questions today. Hopefully we'll finish today, but I'm not that sure. So may I remind you that you're still testifying under oath, pursuant to your solemn declaration. They will continue with other cross-examinations. I don't know what's the arrangement amongst the Defence teams, who is going next. Have you talked amongst yourselves? Madam Fauveau, please introduce yourself to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, my name is Natacha Fauveau Ivanovic and I appear for General Miletic here. Is it correct that in 1995, you were in charge of security organs of the brigade when --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And General Miletic did not call you at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not call me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when in July 1995 you were in the field with your commander, you did not communicate with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Last Thursday, you spoke of humanitarian convoys, and you mentioned a liaison officer with the UNPROFOR. Is it correct that this liaison officer in fact transmitted information to the duty officer who later put it in his logbook?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our command we had an officer for liaising with the UNPROFOR, and his task was to, following orders from the superior command, meet UNPROFOR forces at Karakaj pass and to follow instructions of the superior command, again, in inspecting and checking the convoys in keeping with the inventory announced previously by the convoy as being brought into the territory that we controlled. After that, he would incorporate it into his daily combat report - I think it was item 4 or 5 - saying that the convoy passed at such and such a time and returned at such and such a time. And of course, he would report any problems and sometimes asked for instructions on how to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to correct the transcript. It's page 6, line 19. I was talking -- I said that the witness was in charge of operations and it's recorded as security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the answer now, I think it's the case of putting your question again and the witness answering again, because as it is on the record, he has answered no to a question whether he was in charge of security at the time. So I suggest that -- I don't know, I'm not in a position to know how it was translated, so perhaps you can put the question again, please. Sorry for this, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to ask you one question again because there is an error in the transcript. Is it correct that you were in charge of operations in 1995 and, as such, you had no contact with General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as an operations officer at the command of the Zvornik Brigade, had no contact with General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to go back to the humanitarian convoys and show you 3D -- that is, 5D355. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please confirm that this is in fact a report from the Zvornik Brigade dated 28 June 1995? It is a daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a daily combat report addressed to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the bottom of the page with paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that in paragraph 10 we find information concerning the convoys?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely in this paragraph we see that. Sometimes, as I said, it could be included in prior paragraphs, but since here we have a lot of such information, paragraph 10 contains data on the convoy that returned from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, in fact, this convoy returning from Srebrenica had departed for Srebrenica the previous day and now it was returning to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every convoy was recorded when it passed on the way to Srebrenica, and the time of its passage on the way to Srebrenica and on the way out of Srebrenica were both recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The last paragraph of this item 10 speaks of a convoy that passed on the way to Zepa at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it includes also the composition of the convoy. It confirms what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the Witness 5D354. Can we first show the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that this is a regular combat report dated 27 June 1995, emanating from the Zvornik Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a regular daily report from that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show paragraph 10, lower down the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, in fact, in paragraph 10 we see the same convoy that was mentioned as leaving the territory of Republika Srpska. In this report, it is recorded as an entering convoy passing on the way to Srebrenica at 1310.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that you also indicated in the report when a convoy appeared at a check-point without being announced first?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All incoming convoys that appeared at the check-point were notified to the superior command, that is, the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Similarly, if some goods were removed from the convoy, that would also be noted in the report.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be noted. But before the goods were removed, approval was sought and a confirmation from the superior command that the goods may be removed because they were not on the list that they had to submit in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So if a report says that a convoy passed on the way to Srebrenica, that means that the convoy, as it presented itself with all its goods, was released towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unless there were some other problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I need your advice. I have 48 reports of the Zvornik Brigade from 8th March to 28th June concerning convoys. I consulted the OTP and I informed my colleagues from the Defence. In order to save time, I wanted not to show these reports one by one to the witness; I wanted to tender them in a batch after this testimony. I don't know how the Chamber wants me to proceed. Should I present them one by one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your position on that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Really, there are two things. First, I'm not sure if my colleague is -- I think she sought a translation of all these documents, but they are not translated as yet, as I understand it. The issue with respect to the tendering of all these documents as a batch I had spoken to Mr. McCloskey about previously and I don't think we have a problem with, in principle. The question, though, relates to how the witness's testimony bears upon them and to -- I don't know whether or not my colleague is going to attempt to have the witness verify certain information with regard to the documents as a whole, such as the nature of the reports, I don't think is a problem, but with respect to specific contents of the reports, then it could be. And if she has a specific issue, I think she should address that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That, of course, we will have to wait and see. But on principle, I suppose there is no objection to have them tendered as a batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later on, if as we go on, as we proceed, there are problems, then of course we will discuss and, if necessary, reverse our decision, if that's the case. So that's the position and you're free to go ahead on that understanding, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Of course, I will ask for these documents to be marked for identification pending these translations and admission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke last Thursday about how you proceeded in the brigade when you received from the superior command an order to attack or any other order on which you worked. Could you please explain what was your role and the role of your organ, the organ of operations, when the Zvornik Brigade was preparing a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organ called operations that I headed, as an Assistant Chief of Staff, together with the Chief of Staff and my subordinates and with the assistance of other staff organs, prepared all combat documents related to the concept and idea of the commander related to a specific combat mission. Later on, during combat activities, I monitored them, and before that I monitored the degree of preparation of units in relation to that combat mission, before following the combat activities themselves as an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask for 5D400. This is a document that emanates from the brigade command -- actually, it is relative to the brigade command. Can we please move to page 4 of this document and the same page in the English version, please. Can we move on a bit lower down the page. Actually, the part that I'm interested in is the passage that is now on the screen. Can we actually show the entire passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, could you please read, on this page, what the role and duties of the operations officer were.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read the whole of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. But please read it for yourself. You don't have to read it aloud, actually.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is actually what I've just talked about.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you please explain for the Trial Chamber one very specific sentence, a sentence which reads: "[In English] It is present that the commander takes decision and it shapes them." [Interpretation] Could you please tell us what is the meaning of "shaping decisions"? What does that imply?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For every activity, the commander has an idea what to do and passes a decision as to what will be done, and the operations officer, together with the Chief of Staff and the assistants of the Chief of Staff, transform into a document that later on will serve to provide for an efficient command and conduct of a certain operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You personally and the body that you were in charge of, did you play a role in the decision-making process?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was the one who made all the decisions, as a matter of principle. The assistants and the Chief of Staff could only assist the commander in shaping of the final decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when it comes to you and the body that you were in charge of, you came in later, when the decision had to be shaped and elaborated.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The decision had to be elaborated, and when this was done, it was forwarded to those units that were referred to in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness 5D399, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, here we have an order for defence and active combat activities, number 7/1, dated 8 April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At the beginning of the document it says that this order was sent to the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to see this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could read all of it, then I would be able to tell you. Since I'm not in that position, I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I please give the witness a hard copy for him to peruse. I believe this would be faster than providing a copy in the e-court. After having done that, maybe the witness will be able to tell us whether he remembers this document or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem with that. The only thing that comes to my mind is whether everybody else will be able to follow. If it's put on the ELMO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a problem with the document being shown in e-court, page after page, but I believe the document will be able -- the witness will be able to recognise the document at first glance when he was all of it in his hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Madam Fauveau, as for the previous documents, the brigade command and duties of its organs, do you have any idea what the document was? Was it a rule, an order, or anything else? And when was the document dated?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this document was used in the Blagojevic case, and I found that this document emanated from the Zvornik Brigade, and that it was used at the time. But this is the information that I have based on the Blagojevic case. Actually, it is a book of rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it, if you will allow me to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did you ever see this document before? Especially, did you see it in 1995 or, to be more precise, in April 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I see here that tasks were issued to the units of the Zvornik Brigade, and I really don't remember that we ever received an order in this form, where the Zvornik Brigade would be tasked with advancing along these axes to reach certain lines which are rather far from the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade, I really don't know whether the Zvornik Brigade would be capable to move its forces to these lines, along these particular axes. In other words, I'm not familiar with this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that, as the operations officer, you played no role with regard to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't play any role.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you didn't have any responsibility with regard to the civilian population in the area where the combat had just ended?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Last Thursday, you told us that the brigade was responsible for the area of defence and the buildings that were mobilised for the brigade. If a building was mobilised, were you consulted as an operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As required by the brigade command, certain facilities in the area of defence of the brigade were mobilised through the Assistant Chief of Staff organisation and mobilisation. This was done through a request sent to the Ministry of Defence, and pursuant to these requests, we would either get a building or not, which rather depended on the approval of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But as an operations officer, you did not play any role in the mobilisation of such buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As an operations officer, I did not have a say in that, nor could I request mobilisation of a facility for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You were responsible to the Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade, Dragan Obrenovic. You reported directly to him.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when Dragan Obrenovic was not in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, you stood in for him.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never played the role of the Deputy Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you exercise these activities when he was not in the area of responsibility of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case the commander was not in the area of responsibility of the brigade, or the Chief of Staff, in certain cases I would assume the command of the brigade units, but only in those cases when both of them were absent from the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that actually these were exceptional cases because, according to the rule, it was customary for the most senior officer to assume such responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the rule. However, in our brigade, we somehow changed that rule and I would be the one to assume those responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And since Dragan Obrenovic was not in the area of responsibility -- when he was in the area of responsibility but not in the headquarters, you did not have to stand in for him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when the commander and the Chief of Staff were not in a position to command over the brigade, in certain cases only.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And together with your commander, you would tour the grounds during the Srebrenica operation in June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you also went with your commander to Krajina in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Actually, it is absolutely normal. It was normal that the commander took his operative officer to tour the ground when combat started.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Last Thursday, you spoke about the duty operations officer. You told us that in certain situations he had responsibility for the tasks that had to be carried out. I would like to show you a document that you've seen already. This is P699. This is an instruction for the work of commands and staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown page 36 in B/C/S and 34 in English. Page 36 in B/C/S, please. Can we show the witness article 65 or item 65, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not going to ask you to read the whole paragraph because you already read it. You did it on Thursday. But what I'm going to ask you is to look at the bottom of the page, which is the duties of the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I would like to move to the following page, please, where that is contained. Can we go to the very top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you please read this passage, passage 66.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to read aloud or shall I do it for myself?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please read it for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To follow the course of combat activities and to enter all the changes in subordinated and neighbouring units in the maps; to report to the commander or Chief of Staff about the important changes or the orders of the superiors that require commanders' decisions; to be familiar with the deployment of the elements of the command post, the post where the command is located, the Chief of Staff and assistants commanders as well; to control and maintain connection with the operations duty officer of the superior and subordinated command; to receive and dispatch orders and reports when other bodies are on vacation or when this is ordered to him; to inform about the orders of the subordinated bodies, reports and information by the subordinate neighbouring units, organs and organisations of the DPZ, DPO and OUR, which are relative to the logistics. He informs the PKPO, i.e., the certain organs at the forward command post. He monitors and checks the measures of security and defence of the command post, and in case of attack he sounds alert." These are the duties of the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This will do. Thank you. Is it correct that, according to this instruction that you have just read out for us, i.e., the book of rules, the duty operations officer was not responsible when it came to the performance of tasks; that he did not have any responsibility in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was responsible for monitoring all the tasks and to inform the commander or the Chief of Staff about the degree to which the tasks were carried out. In the Zvornik Brigade, if he did not have a connection with the commander or the Chief of Staff or the duty operations officer, he did have responsibility to deal with certain situations himself and to assume responsibility in a certain way, i.e., to assume the command responsibility to a certain extent. That was the case in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On two occasions, you've told us that this was the case in the Zvornik Brigade, and you were aware of the fact that the Zvornik Brigade was an exception when it came to the responsibilities of the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that we made an exception to the rule because the brigade was outside of the formation and establishment. At every moment we had to know how to deal with the problems if the duty operations officer were not connected to the commander or the Chief of Staff, i.e., not for a single moment did we leave the brigade without a command. We should not have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, the document you referred to as rule, was it not a manual of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge, this is a document issued by the JNA originally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not arguing that document was in effect at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you document number 7D442. This is a document that you have already seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we blow up the title page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the document and can you please confirm that this is a document that was issued by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is our document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now go to page number 4 in this document? Could we please look at the last part of this page. I'm interested in the last three lines on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like you to look at item 6, but only the last three lines in which you can read that the duty operations officer is subordinated to the brigade commander. Is that correct? Is it correct that this is what it says in the document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says so in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And are you in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty operations officer is subordinated to the brigade command, and the brigade commander can order -- yes, I agree. I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the witness page 7 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that paragraph 4 speaks about reporting? Chapter 4, that is, is it about reporting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please read the second sentence on that page, the sentence which talks about different types or categories of information.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What sentence do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm talking about the third line, the sentence that is in the third line which starts with, "For that reason the information ..." and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That is why the information is divided into command information, information on the situation, information on cooperation, and information on neighbouring units."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you to read paragraph 3, the paragraph that talks about information on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Situation reports have the purpose of familiarising with the combat situation concerning units, providing more or less detail. Those are reports and briefs or information."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we say that the daily combat report fell under the category of situation reports?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because daily combat reports also contained an item covering the situation both on the front line and in one's own units.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 10 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have already seen this page last Thursday, and you said it contained instructions on how to compile regular combat reports. I would now like you to tell me, point by point, who provided duty officers with such information. For instance, who provided the duty officer with information concerning the enemy?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Zvornik Brigade, enemy-related information usually went from the Chief of Staff, the operations officer or the commander, or rather came from these, Chief of Staff, operations officer or the commander, or anybody else who was able to monitor the activities of the enemy, and it flowed in at the desk of the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that it came from the operations officer, but he also had to receive it from somebody. From whom?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's usually battalion commanders, artillery battalion commanders, and other unit commanders that were in touch with the enemy, in contact with the enemy, who provided this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And who provided information on point 2?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: State of combat-readiness, usually the Chief of Staff and the operations officer provided that information, because it was the Chief of Staff's responsibility to monitor the combat-readiness of units at all times, together with the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, in fact, it was a responsibility that falls under the responsibility of the operations organ.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell me who provided you with information on the situation in the territory of your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in the area of defence, although the term often used was "area of responsibility," but it was not in the spirit of our rules, since that was the area of deployment of units, all that information flowed in from commanders of battalions, artillery battalions, and other subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And concerning irregular, extraordinary events?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning extraordinary events, information would be provided by security organs, and such events are precisely linked to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And on point 5, state of security and morale?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs provided that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how about logistics?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's a transcript error or something else, but I have to ask you again. Concerning logistics, who provided your information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, sorry. It was the assistant commander for logistics. It was my slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What about point 7, losses?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant Chief of Staff for organisation and mobilisation, because all the information on losses flowed in to him, and he received assistance from the organ for morale, religious and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How about conclusions, provisions and decisions? Who provided that to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander, Chief of Staff or the operations officer could provide that, or the duty operations officer himself could write that, if he was unable to receive that information from the commander, Chief of Staff or the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if he receives that information from the operations officer, how does the operations officer himself get it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations officer, Assistant Chief of Staff for operations, follows the situation, and if the Chief of Staff or the commander are not there, the operations officer, together with the duty operations officer, can make some conclusions, can anticipate, if he is in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that the commander or Chief of Staff are not there, you mean that they are completely outside the area of responsibility of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may be in the area of responsibility of the brigade without being accessible as a result of combat operations or any other elements that make it impossible for them to communicate, and we have to send our report nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But in any case, when the commander and the Chief of Staff are present at the brigade, it's not up to the operations officer to determine the conclusions, to anticipate, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This only happened in situations when there was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the last point, requests or requirements, who determined that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Requirements were identified by the commander or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to go back to point 2. We said that it was one of the responsibilities of the operations officer, but isn't it true that the operations officer always received his information from battalions on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battalion commanders were duty-bound to provide the duty operations officer with reports on the situation within their battalion or any other change that occurred within a certain time interval. Commanders of battalions or artillery battalions did not have to wait a certain set time in order to send their reports. They would send their reports when some changes occurred and when a report was called for.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that if the persons who were required to provide information to the duty officer did not provide that information for some reason, the duty officer could not write up an exact and accurate report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, if he does not have at his disposal information that reflects the actual situation, he could not write a proper report reflecting what is actually happening within the brigade, and it would not be a valid report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So if one of the organs or the units who were supposed to provide the information to the duty officer provided inaccurate information, isn't it true that this inaccurate information would find its way to the superior command through these reports?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could happen that inaccurate information is included in the daily report, if the duty operations officer is unable to verify the information, if he has any suspicions he wants to check. But if he's unable to check, it can easily happen that an inaccurate report goes up to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that the duty officer could verify information received, what were his actual capacities to verify?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the duty operations officer has communication with subordinated units, both radio and wire communications, he could always check the accuracy of the information if he has any suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But if the person on the other end confirms that the information is accurate, although it isn't, the report would then go as such to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would. But then also an interim report could be made to correct that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said last Thursday that in your organ, you were abreast of all the developments within the brigade. Isn't it true that in fact you received only information that was necessary to discharge your functions, that is, information concerning planning, preparation and execution of combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes, but in the command of the Zvornik Brigade, in view of its establishment and all the other factors we mentioned, the operations officer actually had much more information than strictly prescribed by regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But in any case, you did not know, and you were not supposed to be aware of, the quantity of fuel in your brigade or the fate of the prisoners who were in the area of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I did not have to know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said last Thursday that you heard that an officer from the superior command, and that's something you heard when you returned to the headquarters in July 1995, you heard that an officer named Trkulja had come to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you also said that he had taken the information he needed and then returned to his command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that you were not present when Officer Trkulja visited the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present. I just know, I have information, that he had been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in reality, you personally don't know if he had obtained the information he had come for.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I suppose he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I ask for your leave to consult with my colleagues. Just a minute. With my client, sorry. It will take only a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. I have on my list the Nikolic Defence team, who requested about one hour. Madam Nikolic, if you could introduce yourself to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dragutinovic. My name is Jelena Nikolic and I appear for Mr. Drago Nikolic. I would like to ask you some questions concerning your earlier testimony. You testified about the way the brigade was organised, how responsibilities were divided, and about the role of certain sectors. In 1995, were intelligence and security affairs in the brigade divided between two different sections?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was only one section that was subordinated to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were these two affairs taken care of by two different persons, Mr. Drago Nikolic and Mr. Dusko Vukotic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security was the responsibility of Drago Nikolic, and intelligence was the responsibility of Dusko Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You testified about the relationship between Mr. Drago Nikolic and Mr. Vinko Pandurevic in the period of 1994 and 1995, on the first day of your evidence, and you mentioned certain vague elements in the functioning of security.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show in e-court 3D124. These are instructions issued by the General Staff and signed by General Mladic about the work of security organs. The document is from 1994. Could we scroll down a little so that Mr. Dragutinovic can see paragraph 2, below the subheading, "Instruction." That is paragraph 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, Witness, that in the first paragraph, and I will allow you enough time to read it, we read that depending on the situation, around 80 per cent of their total activity -- so the first paragraph says: "The purview of security intelligence organs of VRS focuses on the linkage between intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks, which, depending on the situation, account for around 80 per cent of their total engagement. The remaining 20 per cent of their activities relate to administrative staff, military police and criminal-legal affairs." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Concerning your particular brigade where intelligence and security affairs were divided, in other words, they were led by two officers, two assistant commanders, can we say that 40 per cent of activities and engagement were accounted for by intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot go into percentages and how much of the activity was accounted for by one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But what about the remaining 20 per cent from this paragraph that speaks of administrative staff, criminal-legal affairs and military and police affairs? Do you agree that these affairs are under the command responsibility -- under the commander's responsibility and Chief of Staff's?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's less than what is accounted for by intelligence organs and security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: All right. I would now like to move to another area, the role and position of duty operations officer and the books that he kept.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the duty operations officer entered all information into records, and that information flowed into his office while he was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And that information came directly from sources.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the Witness P377. It's a Prosecution exhibit from the 65 ter list. P377. Page 131. And it's 12 in the English translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, would you be so kind as to look at a little asterisk in the first line and we see the word "Premier." Can you read this.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Premier is our radio reconnaissance centre that performed surveillance on radio communications of the enemy."

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And then there is a dash and some text follows. Can you read it for us.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Scroll it up, please, the top of the page. "Premier - entered and removed two mines, penetrated our positions between dugouts." So our radio reconnaissance centre says that somebody, supposedly the enemy, entered and removed two mines and penetrated our positions between dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So Premier is the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show page 132 of the same exhibit. For those who are following in English, it's page 13. Further down, please. That's all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, we see something similar here. It says, "Palma 2 -" followed by some text. Further below, "Premier -" followed by some text.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My question is, does this also reflect that Palma 2 and Premier were the sources of information recorded by the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are the sources of information, and on that basis the duty operations officer recorded the information that follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another page, 130, please, in B/C/S, and page 11 in English. The top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, could you be so kind as to read, if it's legible. It says, "Security officer forward command post," that is "IKM -"

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says, "Security officer IKM - behind our back at Krizevic. Shooting is directed at Potocari."

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that the source of this information is some security officer located at the forward command post in Kitovnice.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That could be somebody who is either a security officer or performing the duties of duty operations officer at the forward command post, according to a plan, a roster. So he cannot be there by accident. This information tells us that he's a security officer. That's how this text should be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 127, to conclude this series of questions, and to confirm that the date is 14 July 1995. Page 127 on this exhibit. Can we enlarge it a bit, please. Zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the top left corner, we see the date.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This comes from a notebook where everything was recorded in order to be copied later into the logbook of the duty operations officer. It does look a bit fuzzy, but it's legible. It's the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, this was page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honours, it may be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Madam Nikolic. We'll have a 25-minute break, starting now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that there are no further problems with your computer system. You are okay, all of you? I mean you are able to follow what's happening without any problems with your monitors? Okay. Do let me know immediately if there are problems, please. All right. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Again, good morning, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to some more questions with regard to the duty operations officer in the brigade. Tell me, please, the assistant commander for security and the other assistants, did they regularly assume the duties of the duty operations officer in the brigade and elsewhere, according to the rota system?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no exceptions in the Zvornik Brigade. In other words, everybody had to do it. They could serve as duty operations officers at the command or at the IKM, obviously not at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the entries in the duty operations officer's notebook, if somebody asked for the commander or the Chief of Staff --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: -- would the duty operations officer have to enter that, whether this was entered, whether the entries of such type were made?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? If somebody asked for the commander or the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, yes, it was recorded, who was it who asked for them, in order to be able to inform the commander or the Chief of Staff who had asked for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If something urgent happened and if that person insisted on several occasions to speak to the commander or the Chief of Staff, would that be registered, if that person insisted on several occasions on talking to them regarding an urgent situation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty operations officer always recorded the name of the person who wanted to talk to the commander or the Chief of Staff. He had to know exactly who it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would that also have been the case if somebody arrived at the building, if he came to the duty operations officer's office to ask for the commander or the Chief of Staff on the condition that the person did not belong to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same would apply. His name would have to be entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And especially if that person talked to the duty operations officer asking for the commander or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you something about the reporting by the commander. You have testified about the existence of the so-called regular morning briefing where the commander, the Chief of Staff and the assistant commander were present. In addition to that, did you also have monthly briefings or biweekly briefings which would involve a larger number of people?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was the so-called briefing of the battalion and division commanders that could have been attended by the assistants of the commander, and obviously the Chief of Staff and the operations officer were there as well. But this didn't happen every two weeks. It happened as per requirement, when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would that briefing be also attended by the assistants to the commander and commanders of the company of signals, police, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Just the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Only the commanders of those special units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commanders. If those units were independent, if they were companies, then their commanders could attend as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And then they would brief the commander directly about the situation in their respective units and they would convey the orders that had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody participated in such briefings and they would brief the commander on their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the military police unit was Miomir Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And he was the commander of the military police company?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The use of that company for certain purposes, for certain operations in terms of their number, was something that he would advise the commander on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And finally, the order of the engagement of this company would be passed by either the commander or the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if the police units participated in an operation within the framework of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In that sense, the chief of security was the advisory organ to the commander when it came to the use of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I've already explained that there was another aspect involved in that, and that the chief of security had a different role with regard to the police -- military police company.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. With regard to the organisation of the brigade, did any of the assistants to the commander or Chief of Staff issue any orders to the battalion commanders? Were they in a position to do that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Save for the commander and the Chief of Staff, nobody could do that, save for in very exceptional situations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were not in a position to issue any orders to the battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if the commander and the Chief of Staff were not there and the situation required an urgent order to be issued to a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And that would have been considered a very special extraordinary situation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only case. Otherwise, I was not in a position to issue any orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Which also applied to other assistants. They also were not in a position to issue any orders.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. They could not have issued any orders to the commanders of battalions or divisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something about the activities that took place in September 1995, when you testified on Friday, on pages 12791 and further on about the establishment of the Drina Corps Brigade and its activities in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The brigade that was under the command of Mr. Pandurevic returned from Krajina in mid-September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And it was replaced by a new Drina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A new brigade had been established from the units of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic and Witness, please slow down because you are creating problems for the interpreters. Thank you. Particularly you, Mr. Dragutinovic. You need to allow a short interval of time between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise for that. Can the witness please be shown Exhibit number 3D165.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before the document appears on the screen, I would like to tell you that this is an order by the Drina Corps ordering the establishment of a new Drina Brigade, dated 9 September 1995, which was to replace your brigade in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document please be enlarged as to enable Mr. Dragutinovic to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document and tell me whether this is indeed the document that we have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen this document before, but, yes, it originates from the command of the Drina Corps, obviously, and it is addressed to the Zvornik Brigade, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before the words, "I hereby order," it says, "With a view to provide for the time of rest of the 2nd Light Infantry Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, and the change-over was carried out pursuant to this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move the document upwards so we can see the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This brigade was under the command of Major Mirko Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember, but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It says: "The command of the brigade," under A.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at line 7. It says that "NBN, the intelligence will be in the hands of Lieutenant-Colonel Drago Nikolic from the 1st Zvornik Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. And we also had an occasion to see each others on the ground in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 4 of this document, the last page there, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, could you please read under bullet number 12. Can you see what it reads there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The change-over of units and the take-over of the position should be carried out on the night between the 14th and the 15th September 1995."

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that this unit arrived in order to replace your brigade during that night between the 14th and 15th of September, 1995, in the village where you met them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit arrived in the village of Ramici, and on the 15th, in the morning hours, it took up the positions. This is when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit P379. This is the second part of the notebook of the duty operations officer. I would like to look at page 115. I don't think that we have the English translation of that as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, can I draw your attention to line 22 of page 37. Is "Lieutenant-Colonel" right?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to thank Judge Kwon for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was Mr. Drago Nikolic's rank at that moment? Was he a lieutenant-colonel or second lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a second lieutenant, not lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have corrected the mistake in the transcript in this way. I apologise. Can we go back to the document that we had on the screen a minute ago, in order to answer Judge Kwon's question. I would like you to tell us what it says in the document with regard to Mr. Drago Nikolic's rank. The document is 3D165.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can Mr. Dragutinovic now read what it says on line 7.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Second Lieutenant Drago Nikolic."

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And that is the same person from the Zvornik Brigade, Drago Nikolic from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the document that I called for after this one. We said that it was the notebook of the duty operations officer. The number of the document is P379, and the page number is 115. Can this be enlarged to make it easier for the witness to read the page. Could we move the page up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, it is indeed the 14th of September, 1995, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This document has been shown to you before, in cross-examination. Could you please read the line that begins in the manuscript, "Replacement units ..." are the first words. Could you read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Replacement units, 2nd Krajina Corps," I think it says, "departed at 11.20 from the perimeter." The perimeter of the barracks is meant. And then a telephone number and so on. If it's of the 14th, that means the unit departed at 11.20.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The unit we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if the date is the 14th September.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The unit that went to replace your brigade, commanded by Mr. Mile Kosoric and that was established by virtue of the document dated 9 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the past few days, you also testified about a report made on 18 July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: -- by the commander. Several questions were asked concerning the large number of prisoners that were located in the area of the Zvornik Brigade in July. Today, in response to a question from my colleague, you answered that the issue of prisoners was not within your purview as an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: However, what I would like to know is this: If there is a plan of activities for the brigade for the period that follows, and if a large number of prisoners are scheduled to be brought into the area of the Zvornik Brigade, you would have been informed because that is a fact that you had to be aware of for the purposes of planning any other operation or activity in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If there was a plan for bringing a large number of prisoners into the area of your brigade --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: -- in order to plan further operations, would you, as an operations officer, be informed that something like that would happen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the commander or the Chief of Staff would be notified, and then only me, if there is no way of informing the commander or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest something concerning the transcript, page 40, line 19. The word "if" is missing from my question. I asked "If there was a plan for bringing a large number of prisoners ..." Could the record be duly corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In this report of the commander, the commander expresses his anger and concern because a large number of prisoners were brought into the area of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Because the brigade had no resources for caring for such a large number of prisoners because everybody was on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the command of the brigade did not receive any assignments regarding the accommodation or care for these prisoners, and it wasn't involved in any activities on that issue as a command, from what I could see. Plus the command did not decide on any resources necessary to accommodate the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that such a large number of prisoners posed a great threat to the security for the area of the Zvornik Brigade in case they started a mutiny or attempted to escape.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of prisoners could result in all sorts of unpleasant circumstances for the civilian population, not only the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to one issue related to the duty operations officer. Can I ask you, in view of your experience, in case superior officers from the superior command visit the duty operations officer, is the duty operations officer required to obey them and meet their demands unquestioningly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the duty operations officer would have to notify the Chief of Staff and the commander of the brigade of the presence of these officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And if they were not there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then he would receive orders from the superior commanders and he would take the necessary steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Especially if the commander and the Chief of Staff were absent?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and if he is not able to communicate with them. They could issue orders in writing or verbally, and he would have to take some steps and activities in keeping with those orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back to your testimony of 14th June this year before this Court. On pages 12648 and 649, when you were talking about the map where all the operations of the brigade were marked - that's P1463 on the Prosecution's 65 ter list - you said you made that map together with Major Mihajlo Galic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a map dated 1993 and it says "Assistant Chief of Staff for Operations and Training." For a while it was Galic and for a while it was me. So that provided for continuity in developing the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Major Galic continued to work on that map with you until the end.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I worked on it after him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He signed his part.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He signed the part that he did and I signed the part on the map that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also testified that on 15 July 1995 Major Galic came to see you in Zlatne Vode, in the field, and transmitted to you the order on further engagement issued by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the afternoon of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he also inform you then on the combat activities led on the 14th and on the 15th involving units led by the Chief of Staff, involving losses, and did he tell you what else happened in the brigade in that period?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
