utterances.text: In the time that we had, of course we discussed those combat activities and the reasons why we went back, so I did receive a summary of developments in the area of defence of the 7th, 4th and 6th Battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So Major Galic visited positions in the field and also performed other duties, not only his own duties connected to personnel.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every officer could perform other duties on orders of the commander or the Chief of Staff, if the circumstances required it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Major Galic also went to tour the battalions and occasionally involved himself in operational tasks.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations section regularly planned activities of the brigade command to inspect battalions, artillery battalions and subordinate units, and all officers were required to tour battalions and other subordinated units individually or as part of a team. The same is true with Major Galic. He was no exception.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Working in the brigade, you had regular contacts with Second Lieutenant Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did Drago Nikolic sometimes stand for the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His position would not allow him to do that. No, no, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would Drago Nikolic represent himself as an officer standing in for the commander to any persons visiting the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Nikolic very well and I am certain he would never do any such thing, unless the commander authorised him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that happening on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic would never hold himself out to have powers greater than given him by the regulations, because those regulations were honoured in the brigade and observed.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Drago Nikolic would never do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move into private session, Your Honours, for a couple of questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- where I would have to mention the names or the name of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If a civilian showed up asking for the commander or the Chief of Staff, like the person we just mentioned, would the duty officer record such a visit in his book?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the commander was absent, yes. If the commander was there, then he could have ushered the person into the commander's office without recording anything, but of course he would first inform the commander that the person was in the duty officer's room.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem with a translation, with the interpretation, actually. Could I have a minute to review page 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just two or three more questions, Mr. Dragutinovic. Did it ever happen, did your commander ever tell Drago Nikolic to execute some Muslim prisoners and did he say, at a meeting in the command, that some officer came from the superior command transmitting Mladic's order to execute Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never present if such a thing ever occurred, so I couldn't tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to question you about an event of 21st July 1995. Do you know that the forces of the 2nd Corps reinforced by manoeuvring forces had attempted an attack at Zvornik with strong artillery support resulting in a lot of civilian casualties but the positions of the brigade remained stable?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 21st of July, and the attack was on the area of defence of the 7th Battalion. On that occasion, they also shelled Zvornik town itself, causing civilian losses.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that occasion three women were killed and around 11 civilians were wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. I remember even the last name of one of the women. I believe it was Nezarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to 1995, do you remember any negotiations led by Vinko Pandurevic with Muminovic concerning a cease-fire and exchange of prisoners, and these negotiations were attended by Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were some negotiations about a cease-fire and an exchange of prisoners, but I'm not sure Mr. Drago Nikolic was present because I wasn't present myself. But I know the negotiations did happen. In view of his position, maybe he was involved. I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: Do you remember that on the 18th of July in the area of Baljkovica, while a column was passing, there was a special agreement between commanders to let through a group of young men in the area of the 4th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that out when I came to the command of the brigade, when I returned to the brigade command. Let me also add, on the 18th, in the course of the day, passage, unhindered passage, was allowed through the area of defence of the 4th Battalion more broadly, and there was even an officer who was assigned to call out to stragglers and groups of stragglers to tell them that they may pass through in keeping with an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few minutes so that I can check the record. I may have another couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just two more questions, Mr. Dragutinovic, to clarify some things in the transcript. On page 34, line 7 to 13, when we were talking about the meetings which were attended by the unit commanders of the special units, would Mr. Jasikovac also attend those meetings? He was the commander of the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in such cases, because the chief of security would be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Maybe this has not been recorded. I asked you about the monthly briefings.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the commanders of battalions and divisions attending, but the staff units were not there. The military police unit, engineers unit, the signals unit, they were not represented, save for in the cases when the situation so required. Those were the so-called staff units, and the commanders of those units were not required to attend the meetings of the commanders of divisions, battalions, assistants commanders, assistant chiefs of staff. They were not required. There was no room for them to attend such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were there any meetings which they did attend, the commanders of these units, I mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no specially organised meetings of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would they have had such meetings with the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they were subordinated to the staff, that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And then the commanders of those units would brief the chiefs of staff.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Chief of Staff could have asked for certain information from them, if that had been the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And then Jasikovac, as the commander of the military police unit, would debrief the Chiefs of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because his unit was also subordinated to the staff directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. With regard to the schematic that we have seen during your evidence, I understood it that the military police unit is a unit that was directly reporting to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then you did not understand the schematic correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, you said that the commander of the military police unit would not attend the meetings, usually. Can I take it that what has been discussed or ordered, decided, at the meeting would be communicated to the military police unit through the chief of security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank, Judge Kwon. Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. Mr. Krgovic, please introduce yourself to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dragutinovic. I am Dragan Krgovic and I represent General Gvero in this case. I'm going to have a few questions for you in order to clarify some answers that you have already provided during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 7D442. Can we have the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You've already discussed this document with my learned friend Mrs. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now please be shown page number 10 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in answering Mrs. Fauveau's questions about item 5 of these elements for the regular combat reports, you have told us that the situation of security and morale was the issue that pertained to the body of morale. I am suggesting to you that two items have been incorporated under one part, the security and the morale.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This must be a mistake which I did not notice before. You can't have the situation with security and the situation with morale. One is security; the other is morale. The security situation has to do with the security of the unit, the organs and commands, whereas the morale is the morale in the units which can be either good or bad, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the security pertained to the organ of security.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Security pertained to the security and morale pertained to the organ for security -- rather, religious issues and morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these have to be separated.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. They can't be together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown Exhibit 5D354.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please observe pauses between questions and answers and slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at this part that is relative -- under item 5.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. Can it be enlarged, please? Never mind, I can still read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here we see the morale, which is a separate part of the combat report.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already explained that. The previous document that we saw, that we drafted in 1993, we must have made a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this item number 5, when it comes to morale, this is within the purview of the organ for morale.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It has nothing to do with the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Whereas the security pertains to the organ of security.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And one more clarification, please. When combat reports were drafted, the information that they were -- that they were based on came from the subordinated units, from their combat reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is information that was received from the grounds, from the subordinated units, units that were subordinated to the commands of the battalions, divisions, or the bodies of the command themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But they were mostly based on the combat reports of the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the reports received from the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these reports came to the duty operations officer, and from there they are taken and they form the base of the combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That leaves the Beara and the Popovic teams, respectively. Mr. Meek -- yes, Mr. Zivanovic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. All my questions have been asked, so I will not cross-examine this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination? Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would have two or three questions that arise from Judge Kwon's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can the witness please be shown Exhibit number 7D622. Can we have the document in B/C/S for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dragutinovic, do you have the document in B/C/S, in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have the schematic, but the words are in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it is in B/C/S. In Serbo-Croatian, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So now you have it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You agree with this diagram. You've seen it before and this is the situation as it was in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is how the brigade functioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the right-hand side, corner, where you see the military police company under the command of Miomir Jasikovac?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And we have a full line leading leftward to the commander, which shows a direct subordination of that unit to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mistake. This unit was a staff unit, just like the signals unit was or the engineers unit. This is where the unit of the military police also belongs to. But the red line from the commander to the security organ and the dotted line, green line, to the military police unit, they are both okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words, the commander was in a position to issue direct orders to the military police unit, and you don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander could command any unit, without any exceptions. Other members of the command could not command any other units but those that they were in charge of, that were in their authority; or, by the function that they performed, they had some connection to that respective unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that the dotted line that follows the fields where you see Drago Nikolic's name, towards the military police, shows the professional part of the work of the security organ and his advisory function.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That part is okay. That part is absolutely okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In other words, Drago Nikolic could not create orders or issue orders to the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You didn't understand me properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: He could not do it on his own. He could not issue orders without the participation of the commander or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, the military police company, Drago Nikolic could issue orders to it, but when it came to the use of that unit within the brigade, the commander or the Chief of Staff had to be aware of that. It would not have made sense if, at certain moments, Drago Nikolic or anybody else, without any consultations with the commander or the Chief of Staff, could not have used the military police unit. Drago Nikolic could not have used the logistics battalion, for example. He could not have used a company -- signals company. By the same token, the military police company could not have been put into use by any other commander, save for those that were in charge of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But this could have taken place only in exceptional cases. In all the other cases, the order came from the command.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only in exceptional cases, where there was no other way to go about things, when things could not have been done differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That basically leads me back to Mr. Vanderpuye. Do you have redirect, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do, as I indicated yesterday, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yesterday, last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Last Friday, sorry. It will be, I think, a little bit more than the half an hour that I had anticipated, in light of the cross-examinations that have also occurred, but I'll get started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break at 12.30 anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I please have P02840 in e-court. Maybe we could just blow up, I think, the caption and the first paragraph, up to the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's from the Zvornik Brigade, from the command, but I couldn't identify each and every document. It is from the command, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, if you would just have a moment and read the paragraph just below where it is indicated, "Personnel Department." That would be on the paragraph immediately preceding the underlined portion on the right.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, strictly confidential number 25-222, dated 7 July 1994, and the order of the commander of the Drina Corps, strictly confidential number 05/1-266, dated 23 August 1994, and with a view to reducing the strength of the brigade to establishment, ensuring efficient command and further combat build-up of the units, I hereby order ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would you just read what's in paragraph numbered 1, designated 1.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "1: Reorganise the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade [of battalion composition], establishment number 111978, into 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, according to establishment number 111979."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dragutinovic, does that conform with your recollection as to when it was that the Zvornik Brigade Light Infantry became the 1st Infantry Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this document very well. But this reorganisation or reforming of the brigade was never implemented, or I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just go over to ERN ending page 787 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just had to check. To the best of my knowledge, this document has not been disclosed to us and it's not on the 65 ter list. We had no notification it would be used in redirect, so I would appreciate it if our colleague could give us a basis for using this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we've been over this issue on a number of occasions with respect to the use of documents on redirect examination. This document is directly relevant to the testimony that was elicited by my colleague, Mr. Haynes, with respect to the characterisation of the Zvornik Brigade in and around 1994 and 1995, specifically with respect to its characterisation as a light infantry brigade. That's the basis of its use, and I think it certainly clarify identifies the issue with respect to the testimony that was elicited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can safely proceed. I don't need to say much, but basically we are at the redirect stage, which is kind of a different exercise than the direct or cross-examination. One cannot always anticipate what documents are going to be used on redirect; most of the time you can't. You can't even anticipate if you're going to have the redirect in the first place. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could just briefly turn to ERN ending -- on this same document, ERN ending 787. It's just two pages ahead. And in the English, I believe that's page 3. In both. I think it's page 3 in both. And if we could just go down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, do you recognise that signature at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the commander's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the commander you're talking about is Commander Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, in fact, this document indicates that the brigade was transformed for the very purpose of ensuring the efficient command of the brigade; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we did not succeed in following entirely that order from the corps command. Our brigade continued to be somewhere in between the infantry brigade and an armoured mechanised brigade, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, just so that we are clear, the document that I've shown you now is, in fact, an order that's issued by your commander, as you've said; right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I ask the witness this question, out of common sense: To transform a brigade into another one, the order should have come from the higher command. The commander of the brigade himself can order -- issue such orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would you like me to put it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can only be done on orders of the superior command. A unit can be transformed following orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it that there should have been another order coming from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should have been another order, and it seems to me, if you showed me again the beginning, it says something like "Pursuant to ..." an order of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I now see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic. You were shown and asked some questions about regular combat reports by my colleague, Ms. Fauveau Ivanovic. Now, in particular, you were asked some questions about whether or not those daily reports could contain erroneous information that might be passed on to the superior command. Are you aware of any such information, erroneous, being passed on to the superior command in a systemic way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any cases of erroneous information passed on to the superior command that might have resulted in any adverse consequences, but I still believe, and assert, that it's possible to include in daily reports passed on to superior commands information that has not been verified, but that information would later be corrected in interim reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so if erroneous information were passed on in these reports, is it your view that, to the extent that they were erroneous, corrections could be made later on, and in fact would be?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once information is verified and found to be inaccurate, it could be corrected in an interim report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Mr. Dragutinovic. A few questions were put to you regarding the role of the Zvornik Brigade in the liberation of Glodjansko Brdo in 1993. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to that operation, was it the case that the liberation of Glodjansko Brdo was among a series of campaigns that were undertaken by the VRS involving the liberation of several other places?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the liberation of Glodjansko Brdo, there followed an operation of the units of the Zvornik Brigade that resulted in the liberation of other places and features.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did those other places include Liplje, Kamenica, Konjevic Polje, Kravica, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, what happened to the mosques in those towns and places?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will emphasise that in the operations of the Zvornik Brigade related to the second liberation, that is, the capture of Glodjansko Brdo, there had been prior combat that resulted in the damage or destruction to some religious buildings, office buildings, residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that pervasive through all the towns that I have named, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember because I cannot be certain anymore in which village, because they were not towns or cities, they were villages, I cannot recall anymore which of them had churches or mosques or places of worship.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What happened to the Muslims that were living in those villages, Mr. Dragutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about 1993, these population centres did not have any civilian population. They had already left. There were only remaining elements of the combat elements of the 4th Operative Group of the BH army, if we are talking about the places you enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you liberated a village that didn't contain any civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the area of Konjevic Polje, there had been operations before that necessitated the withdrawal of the civilian population, so that in 1993, when there were combat operations towards Kravica and Srebrenica, this territory was covered exclusively by elements of the 4th Operative Group of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, Mr. Dragutinovic. You indicated, I think, Friday that you first heard that there were 3.000 prisoners in the area of your brigade on or about the 18th of July 1995. In fact, the 18th of July 1995. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you found out about that from your commander while you were drafting a report for him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you had no idea about that many prisoners being in your area prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know because I was not in a position, in view of all that was happening, to learn about prisoners, especially such a large number of prisoners taken from the 28th Division or the civilian population, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, 3.000 people is a lot. That's about -- a little bit more than half of the strength of your entire brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's not a question. That's a comment. And he's gone really too far now with his own witness. He's asking leading question after leading question and that is just a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. On redirect, you cannot ask direct questions unless, of course, there are no objections, and in this case, there are. Second, I think we are on a borderline here. If you rephrase the question and keep it within the limits of the redirect, that will be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know when your commander found out about these 3.000 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the commander. But after my subordinate officer, who had been at the forward command post, returned to the brigade command, I learned about a conversation the commander had with the former president of the municipality, Branko Grujic, who had visited the forward command post. My clerk, Ljubo Bojanovic, who later moved to the section for morale, religious and legal affairs, confirmed to me that on that day the commander dictated that interim report, or maybe it was a daily report, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, what day are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 962, please, in e-court. I think if we could just scroll down a little bit. Is it two pages? All right. What I'm looking for might be on the next page, if we could go to the next page, please, on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dragutinovic, I'm just going to refer you to what appears to be the third paragraph from the bottom of this document. I'm just going to ask you to look for and let me know if you see a sentence that begins with the words, "Additional burden ..." or "A burden ..." related to prisoners. If you don't see it, let me know also.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just shown to me, I cannot find. I've read this but --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can page up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you just read that into the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I manage, with this handwriting. "An additional burden to us is the large number of prisoners put up in various schools in the area of the brigade, as well as the obligation to provide security and sanitise the terrain."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that your commander was provided with this information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my sources, the commander received it on the 15th, when he was at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And from whom did he receive this information, Mr. Dragutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said before, according to my sources - and that's my former clerk, Ljubo Bojanovic - the number of the prisoners was notified to the commander by the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the treatment of prisoners, was that something that you were trained on or had knowledge about before the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the order from the corps command, there is one paragraph that says explicitly that prisoners were to be treated in keeping with the Geneva Conventions and other provisions, so that all the units involved in combat operations had that order at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the manner in which prisoners were to be handled, was that something that was known to all of the members of the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the order of the corps command and that specific clause, all members of the command should have been aware of that. As for prisoners of the enemy army, the superior command was responsible, so that subordinate commands had to follow orders from the corps command regarding the prisoners. It was explicitly said how they were to be treated, where they were to be taken, and to whom they were to be turned over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And was that known to the members of the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the order was there at the brigade command, so it should have been familiar to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 1309, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Dragutinovic, could you take a look at the sentence again which refers to the additional burden. Last week you dealt with Mr. Haynes, who represents your commander, with various military terms relating to areas of responsibility of zone of defence, et cetera. But from the sentence you're looking at, it says, "Various schools in the area of the brigade ..." as you read it. Can we take it that those schools were in the brigade area? Could you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try. The command of the Zvornik Brigade - and I checked this when I returned to the command as an operations officer, because all the orders are kept in my operations section - did not receive any orders from the superior command regarding the prisoners and their accommodation in Zvornik municipality. And none of these buildings that are mentioned later were in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade. So what did the commander mean here by "the area of the brigade"? He probably didn't even know which buildings were concerned. Therefore, these prisoners were not taken by the Zvornik Brigade and they were not put up in buildings requisitioned for the Zvornik Brigade, nor did any superior officers in the command of the Zvornik Brigade conduct or manage any activities involving the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And concerning this obligation to provide security, the commander probably meant parts of the military police company, and they were superior security organs from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The military police company that was used by superior security organs and assigned to secure these buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be my answer to your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment while I finish this annotation, please, because it comes at the wrong moment. Okay. Twenty-five minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just raise a little matter. It might be better if the witness slipped off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, thank you. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: After we rose for the short break, I became aware of a document which had been served by e-mail at 12.03 p.m., which was a list of documents which the Prosecution proposed to use in redirect. I'm not quite sure when 12.03 p.m. was in the scheme of things. I think it was about five minutes after Mrs. Nikolic made an objection to new documents being produced in redirect, but there it is. But amongst those documents that Mr. Vanderpuye proposes to use, and I think one of them he proposes to use with his next question, are records of intercepted communications. Now, as I understand the position, there is an unresolved issue as to the admissibility of those documents, and speaking for my part, I have studiously avoided using them in cross-examination so far because of the sensitivities of others to their admissibility in this case. It seems to me it would be inappropriate for those documents to be put to this witness whilst their admissibility is unresolved. There is a second point, which is this: From what I can see, they are not communications in which it is alleged this witness played any part, and so one envisages that the form of the question is: Comment upon this and what these two people are alleged to be saying to one another, which seems to me in itself to be a wholly improper way of phrasing a question to your own witness. I just thought I'd raise those two points now. Firstly, in my view, the use of the intercepts in the examination of this witness is at the moment inappropriate because their admissibility is unresolved; and even if that point does not find favour, then simply asking him to comment on what two people may have said to one another when he is no party to the conversation is of itself not a proper way of questioning the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Vanderpuye -- Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On a related matter, I did not rise to my feet earlier on when the Trial Chamber rendered a ruling concerning the use of that document,, but with your leave I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The document to which we complained earlier on, we raised an objection, that it was a document that was not on the 65 ter list. The Trial Chamber rendered a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I did not intervene at that time because Ms. Nikolic is responsible for this witness. However, with your leave, Mr. President, without wanting to interrupt this testimony, after he's finished I would like to address the Trial Chamber, with your leave. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, can you restrict yourself to Mr. Haynes's remarks or objection? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, with respect to the use of intercepted communications, I think the admissibility question is a relevant issue. However, I think also that Mr. Haynes is well aware that the documents in fact have been marked for identification. To the extent that they have been marked for identification, they are an appropriate subject matter for examination as regards a purely evidentiary question. Aside from their admissibility, since they have been marked and they have been identified, authenticated in this case ostensibly by the intercept operators, I don't think there is much of an issue with respect to that argument. However, with respect to the use of the document as concerns this witness and him not being a party to the conversations that have allegedly transpired in these communications, it seems to me to be a perfectly appropriate question to ask him, A, if he's familiar with the subject matter of the conversation, particularly given the nature of his position in the brigade, given the information that he says he has which has come out on cross-examination, and given the nature of the information that he says the commander is supposed to receive from the various units, subordinate organs and other members of the command. So I think it's an appropriate subject matter to ask the witness about. Certainly, if the witness doesn't know anything about the subject matter, then the question would be answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, do you wish to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I've got nothing further to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We do not see any problem with the use of these documents, even though they are still marked for -- I think it's okay now, but let's finish this. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, for pointing that out to us. We don't see any particular problem or legal problem with the use of these documents, even though they are marked for identification purposes, perhaps if only for the time being. The rest of your objection, after having heard what Mr. Vanderpuye had to say, I think it all depends on the kind of question that he puts and then we will take it up from there. My understanding is that they have -- such documents have also been used with other witnesses that had nothing to do with the intercepts themselves. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before we broke, Mr. Dragutinovic, you had commented on the 15th July interim combat report that was prepared by your commander, referring to the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area. Now, if there were such a large group of prisoners distributed in the schools in the brigade area, such as Kula or Rocevic, Petkovci, Grbavci, whose soldiers would come to assist the innocent Serb civilians should they, these prisoners, have escaped?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think I can. It was very long so I'll try to break it down. If there were a large group of prisoners, 3.000 of them, in the schools in Kula, in Rocevic, in Petkovci, in Grbavci, if they had escaped, whose soldiers would address the situation on behalf of the Serb civilians in those places?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are putting me in a situation in which you are asking for my opinion as to who would have had to protect the population outside the area of responsibility of the brigade. It should have been the civilian police, first and foremost, because they are the ones with responsibilities in the parts outside the control of the brigade, i.e., where the brigade units were not deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have, please, 65 ter 1309 in e-court, please. If we could not broadcast these because these are still under seal. I just want to have that up here for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're familiar with the brigade structure, as you've testified before, Mr. Dragutinovic. The 4th Battalion, is that anywhere near the vicinity of Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion had its defence sector which was in the Baljkovica village sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how far was the command of the 4th Battalion from Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the 6th Battalion, is that in the vicinity of Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence sector of the 6th Battalion was in the village of Petkovci, or partly in the village of Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the 5th Battalion, is that in the vicinity of Rocevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion was rather far from Rocevic, some 10 kilometres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: About 10 kilometres, you said?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about the 5th, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And the 1st Battalion, how far was that from Kula?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also about 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if prisoners had escaped from schools in those areas, is it your testimony that that would not be something that your brigade would respond to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, if the civilian population was threatened and the civilian police could not protect the civilian population, then the brigade command should have taken measures in order to protect such population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did prisoners -- let me rephrase the question. Would prisoners at a distance, at most, of 10 kilometres from these brigades, as we've just discussed, represent a threat to the defence lines held by those brigades -- I'm sorry, battalions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prisoners themselves accommodated in the facilities were not a threat for the brigade itself, i.e., its battalions. However, they did pose a threat for the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Dragutinovic. I'd asked you previously some questions about the handling of prisoners and the rules or understandings related to that. I'd like you to take a look at 65 ter number 1309, which should be on the screen in front of you now. The time we are looking for on the printout will be 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe it's at ERN 03216257. So if we could go down to the bottom of the page, we might see it. All right. Can we go to the next page, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to direct your attention to the first part of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Page 2, please. Just a moment. Bear with me. I'm sorry. All right. It's page 3. And if you could -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's at 8.00 a.m. Do you see that reference in the document in front of you now, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it purports to be a conversation between Vinko Pandurevic and somebody else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think, out of fairness to the witness, it ought to be explained to him what this document is, since I think it's highly unlikely he's ever seen it before, and I think the time and the date should be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We fully agree, Mr. Haynes, actually. It's as if you were reading our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is a perfectly fair objection. I will address it. Thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document purports to be an intercepted communication involving your commander, dated the 23rd of July, 1995, at 8.00 a.m. And I'd like you to read down this document to the point where you see what purports to be your commander asking about where to send them.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before. I've never had an occasion to see it. I would, therefore, like to ask you what the date of the document is and I would also like to know the time. It says here 8.00, but I would like to ask you about the time and date in order to be able to place this document in a certain time. I've never seen this document before. And the only thing I can do with it is to comment upon it, I, as Miodrag Dragutinovic, the operative officer in the brigade. I can interpret it for you the way I can and in no other way. Do you want me to read the document for myself or maybe aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe I can put some questions to you and then you can tell me if you can answer.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document is dated the 23rd of July, 1995, purports to be that date, at 8.00 a.m., and purports to involve your commander. In the document, it is attributed to your commander that he said on that date that, "We are still catching Turks. I have some prisoners, I have some wounded, and I don't know what to do with them, where to send them." My question is, relative to that statement: Why would your commander be saying that he doesn't know what to do with prisoners if that was something that was known to the command?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think he ought to be allowed to read on a little further. This is just a misleading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness and usher, if you could slowly -- Mr. Dragutinovic, I would like you to read what you can see on the screen for the time being, and then as you read through, we will continue scrolling the text up so that you can -- or down so that you can continue reading the entire document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to claim for a fact. For example, there are some names here that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the circumstances that are being spoken about here?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that on the 22nd or the 23rd, there were talks about an exchange of prisoners. This was initiated by the other side because there were people missing on our side for whom it had been established that they were on the BiH army side. And as we scoured the terrain, we also came across some imprisoned members of the 28th Division that we brought to our barracks. We established communication between their side and they wanted an exchange to take place at the local level. But I believe that the brigade commands did not have the right to exchange prisoners at a local level and I believe that this is the context of this document. That's why the commander wonders what to do with the prisoners, whether to wait for the commission that existed in the superior command and that was in charge of exchanges. I believe that I authored a similar document, actually part of a combat report, in which we asked the same question; namely, what to do; how much longer should we wait for the commission? If the document that you showed me a few days ago, bearing a similar date, then I believe that these two documents cover the same event, I would say, because the commander certainly knew how to treat prisoners of war. Those that we had brought to the barracks, we would keep them there for a day, and then from there we would send them to the collection centre in Batkovici. This is a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to another part of this same conversation, your commander refers to a problem of sending wounded to the Zvornik hospital. Are you aware of what problem it is that he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say. At our command we had an out-patients clinic for the slightly wounded. They were our soldiers who were kept there for a while and then discharged to go home. This did not provide any room for prisoners of war. No wounded prisoner of war could be treated at our barracks, so I really don't know what this could be all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that's why the question is being posed, the question being what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of whether or not there were wounded prisoners that were housed and kept in the barracks at your brigade in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that something that you would have known about had it, in fact, been the case, given your position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should know but I don't. I don't know whether there were any at what time. I really am not able to say anything to that. I can't comment upon that. It says here in one sentence whether the letter has arrived for the wounded to be sent to the hospital in Zvornik. "We have a problem and we need a solution today," so on and so forth. This is what it says in the document. In other words, either the commander thinks that a letter has arrived or somebody tells him that a letter should arrive about the wounded being sent to the hospital. My interpretation would be that, yes, there was a problem, and a solution is being awaited.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could, let me just refer you to 65 ter 1310.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Also, this is another intercept and I would ask it not be broadcast. I'm told it should be 1310C for the B/C/S printed version. This one should appear at 8.05 a.m. Okay. It's at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is an intercept at 8.05 a.m. on the 23rd of July as well. It's at the bottom of your screen there, Mr. Dragutinovic. I wonder if you could read that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to make sure the whole thing is there. Could we check the next page, please. I think it continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read those first two lines on the top of the page, Mr. Dragutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a conversation that follows the one that I previously showed you at 8.00 a.m., and in this conversation, one of the speakers says, "What Vinko and I were just talking about will arrive at your place by 1700 hours. The boss, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, will arrive and say what needs to be done regarding the work we talked about." My question to you is: Have you any idea what this intercept is about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic actually appeared at the brigade on that day, the 23rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know. I don't know about that day. I don't know that Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was in the brigade on that day at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Relative to some questions that were put to you by Judge Kwon, I believe it was, you had mentioned that the superior security -- superior security involvement, security organ involvement in these 3.000 prisoners that were being kept at the school. What information do you have about that? Where did you learn this information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can my colleague say exactly what he's referring to in terms of what part of the witness's testimony he's referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you be more specific? And I also notice Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He has been asked this question before the break and he answered it in some considerable detail, about how he first came to know about the 3.000 prisoners and how he thought his commander first came to know about the 3.000 prisoners. We are going over ground that's been extensively covered in this re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Haynes is mistaken because I don't think a single question has been put to the witness regarding the superior command or superior security organ's involvement in the retention of these 3.000 prisoners, and that is my specific question, not the number of prisoners or where they were housed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I think you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have a specific reference. I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once it has been raised, you need to look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Page 65, lines 21 through 24, it was in completion of an answer that the witness had given in response to a question put by Judge Kwon. The witness stated concerning this obligation to provide security, "The commander probably meant parts of the military police company, and they were superior security organs from the superior command."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So my question to you is: What information did you have with respect to the involvement of the superior command in providing security at these schools?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to information that's available to me, according to information that was available to me, that I had access to, namely, the notes of the duty operations officer and the logbook of the duty operations officer which contain several references to prisoners and their accommodation in various buildings in Zvornik, there are only several names mentioned, names of officers from the Main Staff and the superior command. I had no other information regarding prisoners and their accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What information did you have with respect to the officers is attached to the question of whether or not they were from the superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From their names and positions, I see they were from the superior command. And if you took those notes to read, you would see an entry saying that the duty operations officer from the superior command is looking for such and such an officer of the brigade via the duty operations officer of the brigade. The logical inference is that the person is not currently there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When did you come into this information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon returning to the brigade command, when I had occasion to review the operations logbook and the notes of the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that around the 23rd or so of July? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the date, but that's when I returned. As an operations officer I was able to review all the documentation that had come in, to sort documents, to place them in my files that I kept in my office. So I did have insight into all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I show you 65 ter 341, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dragutinovic, do you recognise this document? It's dated 23rd July 1995 and it's a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document would be dated the same day as the intercept that I last showed you referring to prisoners. I want to give you a chance to read it, but if it doesn't contain any reference to prisoners, can you explain why that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that we are going completely beyond the scope of both my colleague's own examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. There was one issue raised concerning 23 July, and in the end the witness provided an answer. Now he's been asked to clarify it. He's also provided what he knows about the 23rd of July. And now on this basis, my colleague is doing a completely de novo examination-in-chief. The logbook was used in the examination-in-chief. My colleague had all the time in the world; in fact, they used double the time that they were supposed to use with this witness. They've had the chance to use the operational logbook. They've done that. And now he's coming back again with the operational logbook, and then, on this basis, to new documents again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There has to be a limit to what my colleague can do in re-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. What is more relevant is which section of the cross-examination prompts this question on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, there was a very specific question that was put to the witness by Mr. Haynes. In particular, Mr. Haynes put to the witness the question concerning the treatment of prisoners and whether or not the treatment of prisoners conformed with the requirements of the Geneva Conventions. This relates specifically to the treatment of prisoners to the extent that is the subject of an intercept that is dated 23rd July, in which the commander himself says he doesn't know what to do with the wounded prisoners that he has. And the witness has also said that he recalls that that information was entered in a combat report of about the same day date. This is a combat report of the exact same date. So the foundation and relevancy, I think, is clearly established from showing the witness this document as well as the question that was put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you to remove your headphones. He understood me in sign language. Did the witness actually say that he recalls having seen this information in the regular combat report or in a logbook, operations logbook, and notes of the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to check the record just now, but I believe he specifically referred to a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the two are not the same, in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe it's on page 74, line 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fairly long answer but on that particular page and line you'll find the reference to combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. You may proceed, provided you limit yourself to the combat report that you are referring the witness to. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just note for the record that page 75 referred to by my colleague is part of redirect, or 74 is redirect, so it's a question that -- something that came out in redirect and not something that comes from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our reasoning is this: He's just stated a couple of minutes ago, looking at the purported intercept, in answering a specific question, that he also recalls -- it's being put to him that he recalls the same subject matter being inserted in a combat report. My problem was whether it was a combat report or a logbook, as you had indicated, but I think we can move ahead now. So go ahead. Your question, Mr. Vanderpuye, because we've lost track of it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It hadn't arrived as yet because you were interrupted. The question was put: "This document would be dated the same day as the intercept that I last showed you referring to prisoners. I want to give you a chance to read it, but if it doesn't contain any reference to prisoners, can you explain why that would be the case." And that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I want to make sure that the witness has a combat report, because it's in Serbian and I can't read it and I don't have the English translation readily available. It is a combat report. Mr. Dragutinovic, is what you're looking at a combat report, regular combat report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at a daily combat report, but I didn't actually say it was just a combat report. It's a combat report that I wrote in longhand and that contains almost the same thing that is contained in the intercept. That's written in longhand, in my handwriting. I wrote that together with the commander and our demands from the corps are the same, almost the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to stop here for today. How much longer do you have, Mr. Vanderpuye? Because you said half an hour --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and we've gone beyond that considerably. And it's not fair with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I think that a rather substantial cross-examination was conducted by my colleagues and I think that some very important and salient issues have arisen from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we want to know is how much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Assuming I'm not bogged down by objections tomorrow, I think I can do it in probably about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We started with half an hour and we've gone past an hour and a half almost and you need another half an hour. I think you are leading us into a position where we will just block you in an alley with the consequences that what applies for the goose will apply for the gander, and I don't think either side will like it. But unless you use self-restraint and self-discipline, I think you are going to force our hands and we will intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll bear that in mind, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I said this again last Friday. I'm sorry, Mr. Dragutinovic, we haven't finished. But you won't be here for long tomorrow. We will reconvene tomorrow afternoon. The same advisory applies: Please do not contact anybody or discuss with anybody the subject matter of your testimony. The sitting stands adjourned.
